title: Philippine Energy Security Could Determine the Outcome of a Taiwan Contingency
author: Steven Bancroft
text:
A U.S. Marine assigned to I Marine Expeditionary Force transports a fuel hose during a specialized fueling operation in support of Exercise Balikatan 2026 at Cagayan North International Airport, Lal-lo, Philippines, Apr. 25, 2026.
Credit: U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Jade M. Caldwell
In March, a U.S. ally declared a “state of energy emergency” after experiencing disruptions to its crude deliveries. After gaining a waiver from Washington, Petron, the Philippines’ only refinery, bought Russian oil. The episode exposed a decades-old vulnerability in U.S. strategy: Philippine fuel insecurity.Beginning in 2010, across three Pacific tours, I’ve watched China erode regional security through its increased power and aggression. For the United States to deter China from a Taiwan annexation attempt, it requires access to the Philippines and its oil. However, a conflict that draws in the U.S. will likely disrupt the Philippine oil imports that sustain American operations.[...]
